comments.name: Gary Phillips

I supported the idea behind the #MeToo movement because people who report sexual assault deserve to be taken seriously and treated with respect. But I also believe accusations should be thoroughly investigated before public opinion permanently destroys someone's life or career.

In an era where misinformation spreads quickly and public judgment often comes long before the facts are known, we've seen cases where accusations were later found to be false or unsupported—after the accused had already suffered irreversible personal and professional damage.

Something about the allegations against Planter gives me pause. I don't know whether they're true or false, and I think it's important to let the evidence determine the outcome rather than rushing to judgment.

If the allegations prove true, then accountability is appropriate. If they prove false, however, no later correction will restore the reputation, career, or opportunities that may already have been lost.

The case of Al Franken is often cited by people who believe public pressure can force consequences before all the facts are known, regardless of how one views the merits of that case.

And I have questions about who may benefit politically from these allegations or whether they were coordinated by a campaign or outside interests.

Vince and Margaret spent years taking care of Margaret's mother, who had severe Alzheimer's and couldn't be left alone for more than a brief period of time. Other than Alzheimer's, the woman was in robust health, so for probably at least 15 years Vince and Margaret were mostly housebound. When the mother finally passed away, it looked has if Vince and Margaret might finally have the freedom to do more of the things they desired. But then Vince died of a heart attack just a few months later. Sometimes, unfortunately, good deeds go unrewarded.

I am the sole family member taking care of my 101 year old mom. There is the worrying, turning away, tears, frustration, and sadness of watching someone you love diminish. It is a part of life and loving that is not totally unexpected, but still very difficult.

 The hardest part is confronting your own mortality. How will I go? What will my end years be like? How will I avoid not being a burden for my spouse and children in country not for old men or women.

comments.name: Beth H
comments.body: My heart goes out to everyone that is experiencing this. Both my parents are gone, one very fast with cancer and hospice care which was so helpful and compassionate. 10 years later my dad was suddenly at age 91 bedridden. This condition lasted for about 6 months until he passed. My parents had always lived a good life but lived well below their income, so they had money saved up. My sister and I arranged to get him full time at home care and at a cost of about 8-10  thousands dollars a month, we could. We and other family members spent time with him as often as we could but the burden of daily care was  mostly taken care of.  He could have gone into a “nice” facility at an even higher monthly cost, but he wanted to be at home. My point is, people with money will handle this situation very differently then a family that can’t afford thousands of dollars a month. The injustice of income inequality apparent again.

comments.name: TheatreCrazyRedhead
comments.body: I just spent over 15 years caring for my mother - through breast cancer, hip surgery and spine surgery.  She passed this past August at age 99.  My husband was working and living 130 miles away and I "moved back home."  We never thought twice about what our plan would be because we are a very small family. What we didn't realize was all the time, effort, aggrevation, arguments with insurers and Medicare, paperwork, hours on the phone and driving it required. As a Stage Manager in a highly competitive market, a year is a long time to be away from being available to work. 15 years is a lifetime. I was lucky - my mom was extremely sharp and communicative until the end of her life. But, the last 5 years were spent in a skilled nursing facility. That throws another curve ball - finding a reliable and reputable facility (non-profits are best!!!). Then there's the financial aspect. Who will be paying for this? It was a constant source of stress and there was little little help available. While I miss my mom so much, talk to her daily, wear a silver imprint of her fingerprint over ny heart, almost a year after her passing, we are still dealing with "surprises."  This job is not for th weak, that's for sure. If you can get any sort of compensation, go for it!

comments.name: Peter
comments.body:
Thank you for shedding light on this issue. I am caring for my wife, who suffers from debilitating  dementia. Am a 75 year old man thankfully in excellent health. Between the 24/7 needs, fighting with insurance (note: Genworth long term care is loaded with gaps and long interregnums before reimbursement kicks in), vetting in home help so as to get household needs such as shopping done, and getting appropriate care for my beautiful wife during my absence, I feel as if I am in a very slow sinking pond of quicksand. We have no children or close family readily  available for help, and the thought of assisted living would, knowing my wife, accelerate her demise. I also worry about what happens to her if something happens to me.
The very private tending to my once incredibly independent wife who was a concert violist, breaches the most intimate boundaries of what it is to be human. She is totally dependent on me for everything, and with that comes tremendous responsibility and exhausting repercussions. We, although not wealthy, at least have means through hard work all our lives and excellent planning (mostly by her). Yet Even those attributes cannot anticipate the many awful unanticipated issues that arise.Those who have very little means are squarely  in the middle of a terrible nightmare. I can only offer my condolences and empathy.

comments.name: Naples
comments.body:
The current lack of planning for an aging population leaves as big as or more of a financial burden on the "sandwich years" of life, for the middle-aged as child care. We continue with a bygone model based on one spouse not being employed outside of the home which is no longer a reality. Elder care takes time, emotional fortitude, and in many cases erases generational wealth from the middle classes. We know this administration does not address society's needs for elder care, child care, health care, housing or retirement. So we need to talk.

Look to Japan. Japan has the oldest population in the world, more people over one hundred than any other country. They've even developed robots to help. I'm in my seventies—I would rather not end my life wasting away in a poorly-staffed and underfunded nursing home. I'd like euthanasia to be part of the choices for endlife, although I clearly see the religious riots and opportunity for abuse that would need to be addressed. We can work on this.

We can begin to look at the way existing governments are approaching the graying of societies everywhere. Thank you for opening this important conversation. Many people would like an opportunity to leave something of what they have accomplished to their children.

comments.name: JJohn
comments.body:
I gave up 12 years of my life to care for my parent. 15 if you count the years since parent experienced a major medical event before I moved in. (That FMLA leave eventually cost me a good job.) 24 years, if you count the death of paren’s spouse. 

My health is compromised, my body shot. 4 hours a sleep maybe a night for the last 4 years caregiving. 

Sibling for whatever reasons, didn’t help at all. Couldn’t even be bothered to take parent shopping, for a ride  or for lunch. 

Near the end, I had help from a friend and then a wonderful aide. Sibling carried the financial burden for that of which parent and myself were grateful. But not at night. Time, an hour would have been appreciated. 

Federal insurance and LTD policy didn’t provide for in-home care. Ironically the LTD policy with a partnership with NYS, would have paid the entire shot for the nursing home, had parent been willing to go.

My parent was secretive about money. Long before parents need help:

Find out if they have LTD and what it will cover. Have them gather assets and bank info, brokerage info if applicable, what they envision their retirement years to be. Safe keys! Agree on what point a POA should be implemented. Make sure their wills or trusts are up to date. If you have dead siblings, their death certs. 

Find an attorney you both trust. Arrange a meeting to go over what’s required. Anything for the future that can be converted so that you don’t need probate. Annuities are taxable to the beneficiary.

comments.name: ozma207

The National Park Service's "Triumphal Arch at Memorial Circle: Assessment of Effects Report" contains the following claim:
The conceptual origins of the corridor date to the report of the 1901–1902 Senate Park Commission, commonly known as the McMillan Plan (U.S. Congress 1902), which proposed a monumental bridge and axial landscape composition linking the planned Lincoln Memorial with Arlington House, the former home of Robert E. Lee.
This is highly misleading. The 1902 report from the Senate Committee on the District of Columbia, "The improvement of the park system of the District of Columbia" known as the McMillan Plan has no reference to an arch as part of the Arlington Memorial Bridge. The only specific reference to the construction of an arch is this on page 40:
For example, at the head of North Capitol street a monumental entrance to the Soldier's' Home should be built; and the sharp rise of Sixteenth street should carry an imposing arch, such as the one projected as a memorial to William McKinley.
Sixteenth Street in the District has no physical connection whatsoever to the Arlington Memorial Bridge.

https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_Ob7PAAAAMAAJ/page/n110/mode/1up

We've slowly been transforming our 1.5 acre property from lawn to native plants, small sections over time. We also let the leaves that fall from the many sugar maples stay on the ground to help invertebrates survive the winter and provide food for the birds in the spring. We've definitely noticed an uptick in native bees & pollinating insects in general, and birds are always singing in the many trees we have.

Our neighbors razed the forest that used to be behind our house to build their home, and their yard is now devoid of life, and gets very hot during the summer since it has no trees to cool the breezes.

Lawns are over rated.

comments.name: Cactusman
comments.body: The author hails from Portland, Oregon, so  I was surprised there was no mention of the Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation (xerces.org). Based in Portland, Oregon, Xerces provides a wealth of useful information and resources, including outreach events, focusing on native plants for specific geographic areas, especially those that attract native pollinators and cutting the indiscriminate use of pesticides and herbicides. While my yard is by no means completely native, I have used this information to make it more pollinator friendly by eliminating poisons, leaving the leaves, and allowing shrubs and trees to provide cover and shade for birds and other creatures. The most important step is to just start. You will be amazed at the transformation, both in your yard and in you.

My yards, filled with sages, mallows, CA lilac and monkey flowers are a thriving ecosystem filled with bees, butterflies and birds.  As I type,  two white butterflies bobbed on by. I have as well followed the ongoing research around what are the best species that will help us deal with our climate crisis and how to best provide for habitat for biodiversity. IMHO is perhaps the hardest question that is in front of us. The least we can do is help educate gardeners to think beyond the use of ornamentals for their yard, instead, we need to assess our gardens for their positive contribution to the ecosystem. In the Anthropocene, we humans tend to think of us outside of the ecosystem rather than part of it. Much work ahead of us. Thanks for the great, useful piece of consolidated research and information. comments.name: Andrea
comments.body:
Planting native trees and shrubs has really transformed my yard and attracted many birds and other wildlife. My advice is take your time. Over the years it's been very easy and affordable. While I planted some of the trees, many of the native trees in my yard just started growing naturally. So it hasn't really taken as much effort to make the yard a wildlife haven as one would think. I just have to weed the invasives like English Ivy and porcelain berry and nature does most of the rest. Your local county government may have a free native tree planting program like mine does. 

All of that said, I, like the majority of environmentalists, view wildlife-friendly landscaping is a great supplement to the conservation movement, but of course not the solution. Our political focus should be on protecting more federal and state lands from industrial development, promoting sustainable plant-based agriculture over animal factory farms,  promoting more eco-friendly forestry practices, promoting renewal energy, and more. But your backyard is always a good place to start and wildlife-friendly landscaping has been a fun and rewarding hobby for me so I encourage those with any amount of property to get involved with this important movement.

comments.name: A clever name
comments.body:
Ok, wonky stats here, maybe this will help give some perspective...

Less than 4% of REPORTED sexual assault and rape cases result in a conviction. Because many victims do not report the crime to the police, the conviction rate for all actual incidents is much lower. The journey from a crime to a conviction—often called the "attrition rate"—shows a sharp drop at every step: 
Many go unreported: It is estimated that a majority of survivors never report the assault to law enforcement.
Arrests are low: For every 1,000 rapes that are reported, about 18 to 50 result in an arrest.
Few are prosecuted: Only a fraction of arrested suspects face formal prosecution in court.

comments.name: DemocracyIMPERILED
comments.body:
George Will wants you to believe money and speech are the same thing, then hopes you don't notice he never actually proves it. That's the whole argument. Everything else is built on top of that unproven premise.
He's not wrong that shifting money to PACs backfired. $15.7 billion to PACs versus $2.7 billion to parties in 2024 is real, and PACs are more ideologically narrow than parties, so yeah, that fueled polarization. Fine.
But then he picks teachers unions as his example of "appearance of corruption" without mentioning corporate and industry PACs outspend them by miles nationally. That's not an accident. That's picking the one example that fits the story he wants to tell.
And "appearance of corruption" isn't reformer paranoia, it's a legal standard that exists because you can't prosecute a wink and a nod. Nobody hands a senator a check with a note attached. Courts built that standard as a workable proxy precisely because direct proof is almost impossible to get. Will just says "good grief" and moves on like that settles it.
He also never touches the actual research on what unlimited coordinated spending does to who gets represented. Gilens and Page's work on policy capture, for one. You can disagree with it. You can't just skip it and call the constitutional question closed.
Whether you think Citizens United was rightly decided or not, a serious essay defending it should defend the premise instead of assuming it. This one doesn't. It's well written. It's just not the airtight case it's dressed up as.

always love a good microbiome story. too bad they probably dont have the capacity for time courses on their cohorts. i saw an interesting talk recently covering similar ground on attempting to quantify the evolution of the microbiome where they noted occasional flip-flops of dominant microbiome species composition even within “healthy” participants (on the scale of a few months). so they did the natural thing to simplify their data, noted it and looked at the stable populations instead. they also axed antibiotic patients and in addition all “non-healthy” groups. always drives me crazy when people pare down their sample so much, but here i love that theyre taking lifestyle and anthropological data into the record. now if only the depth here could be combined with the breadth of the (almost) daily sampling approach i saw described last week… maybe they could find some fun causative effects.

or maybe they would see they still have no idea. gotta love watching your preliminary trends evaporate with more complete datasets.

The cold plunge that Taffy described causes the body to release the following cold shock proteins:

RBM3, which enhances nerve synapse plasticity and is strongly neuroprotective, supporting recovery from hypothermia.

CIRBP,  which is an RNA chaperone that binds and stabilizes specific messenger RNAs during cold and other forms of cellular stress. (The long-lived bowhead whale’s  genome has been found to massively over-express CIRBP.) 

YBX1, which is involved in DNA/RNA regulation during stress, supports DNA repair, and also supports cell replication.

comments.name: damon walton
comments.body:
Reading that more Americans than ever are taking weight-loss medications really resonated with me because I am one of those success stories. Seven weeks ago, I weighed 302 pounds. Today, I weigh 264 pounds—a loss of 38 pounds in less than two months while taking Zepbound.

  Like many people struggling with obesity, I spent years trying different approaches. I learned that weight loss is not simply about willpower. It involves biology, metabolism, hormones, habits, stress, sleep, and countless other factors. For some of us, medications such as Zepbound help address the biological side of the equation in a way that diet and exercise alone could not.

 What has surprised me most is that the medication is not a magic solution. It is a tool. I still have to make better food choices, stay hydrated, remain active, and be mindful of long-term habits. The difference is that I no longer feel like I am fighting my own body every step of the way.

  Beyond the physical changes, I have noticed improvements in energy, mobility, confidence, and overall quality of life. Everyday tasks are easier, and I feel more motivated to continue improving my health.

  My journey is far from over, but going from 302 pounds to 264 pounds in seven weeks has shown me that meaningful change is possible.

I don’t love the reflux and my mood could be a little more upbeat but I weigh that against losing 18%+ body weight and fitting into clothes that I haven’t been able to wear in 7 or 8 years.

I grew up in a conservative, rural-ish place, where many people (including my family) were gun owners, hunters, and target shooting enthusiasts. In the 1990s, no one I knew thought that AR-15s  were "common" guns. There has pretty obviously been a concerted push to market them to people and get enough of them into circulation that this exact argument can be made before the Court, and I think it's clear that the Court's Republican-appointee majority is in on the game.

Given the Court's new interest in playing armchair historian, perhaps a good argument to the Court would be to present the historical trend in AR-15s as a share of firearms manufactured in the US. They made up about 1% of firearms manufactured in 1990, but about 25% in 2019. Historically, they have clearly not been in common use. But who am I kidding? SCOTUS will have already made up their minds.

comments.name: Devout Skeptic
comments.body:
The court reached a historically wrong decision in D.C. v. Heller. Now legal observers are all excited about how the SCOTUS will decide a case that raises an irrelevant question.

The Court cannot determine the "common use" of an AR-15 without first deciding what "common use" means. Is the common use of an AR-15 what the majority of users do with it, such as going to a shooting range on Saturdays and tearing paper targets to shreds, or is it some plan that exists solely in the minds of the owners, such as being prepared for a popular revolt against our government? If the latter, its "common use" is utterly subjective and impossible to determine.

The frequent references to the number of AR-15s in private hands, such as Justice Kavanaugh's "strong argument that AR-15s are in popular use" in the last paragraph, turn a grave question of pubic safety and order into a popularity contest, thereby depriving the Second Amendment of any serious limitations on gun ownership. If hundreds of thousands of people owned anti-aircraft guns, this argument says, then anti-aircraft guns are ipso facto legal.

I work in an industry that heavily depends on federal regulations.

It may sound paradoxical but businesses often like regulations.  The purpose of regulations is to publicize how the government interprets a statute that it is required by law to enforce.  Not having a regulation most definitely does not mean that the government cannot opt to not enforce the statute. Article II of the Constitution says otherwise.

This provides a more predictable business environment as businesses will generally know how a statute will be applied in specific factual situations.

The government has to interpret the meaning and intent of a statute regardless of whether it writes it down as a regulation. But regulations provide businesses knowledge in advance of the government's interpretation and that the statute will be applied in a uniform and predictable manner.

I'm estranged (their choices) from my 3 children as a result of a very highly contested divorce from a narcissist (enough said).

When acquaintances ask about my children. I say they are all doing well and living great lives.

I say I never ask to visit ON holidays because holidays were made so difficult by one set of grandparents and I vowed I'd not repeat that. (I actually have never met 6 of my 7 grandchildren, nor visited any of my children, holidays or not holidays).

I say that at my adult children's requests, I say very little about them because their dad's mom told her friends EVERYTHING about our family. So when we visited that side of the family, all the friends of those grandparents wanted to rehash our lives. And my children saw how much their dad HATED that. I add they are all doing well and living great lives. (My children have never visited me).

I very, very occasionally refer to my children's childhoods. But never in detail.

So people don't inquire further.

I (now) am very happy to hear about everyone else's children and grandchildren--so I'm a great listener.

It works. And I've done many years of therapy to get to this peaceful place.

Please don't hate on me or encourage me to reach out to them. Been there, done that, unilateral crickets from all three. Repeatedly. Sometimes life is what it is and a person needs to move on.

Thank you and best wishes!

If they press on that point, I simply say that not all of us are blessed to come from families that love us and care for us. There's always a pause, a record skip in their brains. I allow the uncomfortable silence to fill the space. Then I change the subject. If they follow up with why don't I go fix it with my family, I'll say I tried that for 50 years and it's still broken. comments.name: Rufus
comments.body:
FWIW, here's my take on the surge of the far-right, and why the "do something" strategy as outlined in the article will not work.

The fundamental problem is that the standard of living of the "middle class" has been declining for 40 years, and this makes those people very unhappy.  At least in the US (I can't say for UK, FR, GER) the standard of living for the poor, and for the rich, has been *increasing*.   This is very visible, and further irritates the middle class.  The primary causes - automation, communication technology, and now AI - are only going to make these problems worse.

While immigration is not a primary driver of these economic changes, the reality is that humans are deeply tribal, and, if they are already irritated, going out and seeing a lot of people who don't look like them makes them even more irritated.

Finally, 90 years ago, government spending was 2% of GDP, so making some minor moves towards socialism (e.g. Social Security) could be made relatively cheaply.  Now with government spending well about 20% of GDP, getting taxed even more for income redistribution is politically not viable.

The far-right can't solve these problems any more than the center or the left.  They understand this, and their strategy is to give people someone to BLAME.  This is very comforting to the angry masses, even if in reality nothing is being done to fix things.

Migration is finally being addressed uniformly. across the EU  instead of by each of the 27 countries.  It is called the "EU Migration Pact of 2026". These details from "The Human Rights Watch" site: 

- Uniform Border Procedures: Mandatory screening at external borders for identity, security, and health checks. Applicants unlikely to receive protection undergo a fast-tracked border procedure to process claims within 12 weeks.

- Compulsory Solidarity Mechanism: A binding responsibility-sharing system that requires member states to either relocate a minimum of 30,000 asylum seekers annually or pay a financial contribution of €20,000 per unaccepted migrant into a collective "Solidarity Pool"

- Stricter Responsibility Rules: Revised tracking via the Eurodac database to prevent unauthorized secondary movements between EU countries and strictly enforce rules on the "safe third country" concept.

- Expanded Detention and Returns: Faster processing of rejected asylum applications alongside return decisions, which may allow for detention of up to six months during the deportation process.

Thank you to the Washington Post for this insightful essay. 

The general findings are consistent with my personal experience with strength training and cardiovascular optimization as well as maintenance. 

The number one factor is perseverance. In other words….setting your own schedule and sticking with it. It’s about making a personal choice that one’s physical health is important in determining life style quality. Yes there will be days from time to time because of weather or other urgent matters that surface….no self flagellation. Accept this can occur from time to time and just return to the routine the next scheduled time. It’s all about what works for each individual in maintaining consistency and engagement over time.

The other feature….once the exercise becomes incorporated consistently in one’s weekly routine is to gently challenge oneself. 

On the cardiovascular side this means increasing the intensity ( either speed or incline or resistance) such that one is slightly “ out of breath “ or may have a bit of difficulty speaking for 5 min out of every 15 min interval of exercise. 

On the strength training side adjust the weight or resistance so that the last two repetitions in a set of three 10 set repetitions is “ difficult “ to accomplish. 

That’s about it….nothing too complicated. 

One final observation: For some people having an agreed upon time to meet with another person or another small group can help maintaining the consistency.

articles.title: Tell The Post: What advice would you give other parents who are paying for college?
articles.summary: The Washington Post wants to hear from parents who have paid for their child's education and have tips for other families.

comments.name: LoneStarJim
comments.body:
1. Do NOT advise your child to take A.P. courses in High School, it hurts two ways: The more difficult curriculum pushes DOWN their GPA, reducing their college options, and then we found out the hard way, none of the in-state universities within 200 miles recognized / accepted those courses for credit, so they were a double-hit.
2. Make sure your child chooses a realistic goal with a degree in a field that will provide a high paying job. Forget Social Services, Sports Medicine, etc. My son changed majors twice, and fortunately he went with an always valuable program, (Logistics and Supply Management). 
3. He spent the first two years at a Community College, getting nearly all of the General Ed requirements out of the way at a very low cost. What matters is the degree you get in the end, and nobody knows or cares if you only went to the "big name U" for the last 2 years. He graduated with only $20K in student debt, which he has already paid off early.
4. Son chose a university within commuting distance, and lived at home, so he managed to avoid the party scene, the frat life, the added costs of dorm/rent, food, etc. (Yeah, I know some will say "he missed out on college life". Whatever, he moved forward in life, well past his friends who got to enjoy "college life" and now have $50K jobs, and $150K in student loan debt).
My son got an internship during his final semester and was offered a job by that company the week he graduated. That was 3 years ago, and he is already working for a well-known nationwide retailer, making over $160K, and enjoys his work.  
What matters is the result, not the journey. There is NO need for a child to go into debt over $100K to have a prosperous future.

comments.name: anon-ymous
comments.body: Help them all you can, they need more than just financial support, they are called college "kids" for a reason. Tough love doesn't work. Love is gentle, attentive, and kind. Stay in contact with them.

comments.name: Slowfoot

comments.name: Patty DeVille
comments.body:
Just don't until the kid does their research about colleges, expenses, the likelihood their major will support them and their student loans and living expenses after graduation. My son thought he wanted to be a video game designer (in the early 2000s) so I had him research colleges with that major, the cost of tuition, how he would pay, how he would live while in college, the list of classes he would have to take and his options. We toured a couple of colleges. He researched job possibilities and salaries.  And he decided it wouldn't be worth it since chances of a high paying successful career were small. 

Kids need to know the exact cost of going to college, no matter who pays, including the cost of student loans and what happens if parents co-sign and get stuck with the bill. Growing up I was always open with my son about costs and money and "how do we make that happen?" He decided to go with his first plan: join the military. No cost to him and he got a good education, a career, a retirement check after 21 years, and he was young enough to get a fantastic job with a company only hiring ex-military intelligence. He is debt-free, paid cash for a house, and is doing just fine.

comments.name: ConnieConnie
comments.body: Too late for people whose kids will be starting college soon, but try to save at least something before the need arises. Far too many articles about financial aid (or lack of it) assume a family is going to try to pay the sticker cost out of current cash flow which is totally unrealistic for the vast majority of Americans, even the highly compensated. Don't be flummoxed by the idea that you have to pay the list price, and don't believe the hype that you have to prefund $100k in a 529 plan for each college bound child.

comments.name: tayfm
comments.body:
We started 529 plans when our two daughters were in elementary school and contributed every year which also lowered our state tax bill. We didn’t have enough in the 529s to cover everything  when they turned 18 but continued to contribute the 4 years they were in college. As soon as each reached 15 they found jobs, at first part-time and then in the summer, full-time; they knew that the money they saved would be their spending money in college so at least half went in the bank. One complained and wanted to know what happened to that money if she did’t go to college; I explained that would be the money she would use to start life on her own when she graduated from high school.  Each of their junior years,  we let them know what we had to pay for college, which was enough to cover any in-state school (MD).  Then we limited them to a geographic area that was within reasonable distance, 5 hours drive, of our home because we were not paying airfare for college breaks and I doubted they would want to use up their ‘spending money’ on airfare. If they applied and/or received scholarships that would cover a more expensive college that was fine. One ended up at an in-state school and one found an out-of-state school that met the $ and distance criteria (with the help of a small scholarship). They both received good educations and both were employed found jobs quickly.
We also did not buy into the ‘perfect college for you’ talk that goes on in high school. There are lots of colleges where a student can be happy and successful. The ‘perfect college’ label makes young people anxious they won’t pick the ‘right’ one then anxious they won’t get in and if they don’t get into their perceived ‘perfect’ school, they are less likely to be successful at another school and more likely to drop out.

comments.name: CardinalK529
comments.body:
Number one thing is to start saving early for each kid.  Also... we thought they should have some skin in the game, so we filled out the FAFSA forms and got what Gov't loans they would qualify for. For ours, it wasn't a ton but for a 4 year out of state school, they ended up with about $20k in loans.  They each secured some money from the school.  We supplemented with cash. They took dual enrollment courses in HS which turned out to be 12 college credits that were practically free. Took some AP courses. Attended a branch campus of their schools at a discounted rate from the main campus. One had room and board paid for two years while working in the school's Ag dept. taking care of animals. One was home during covid so took courses through the college's online campus at a much lower rate than on campus.  They are still paying their student loans, and once we retire, we decided that we will have something set aside to hopefully either pay those off or reduce them by a lot.
BTW: when we paid the tuition with our funds, we paid using an airline credit card and immediately paid it off and racked up a ton of miles.

He made the city safe to go out in again, by scrubbing off the graffiti, preventing fare evasion, and, yes, making sure that arrests were made and street crime was punished.  He also ran a tighter ship.  He brought in computerized reports that made it possible to see whether the cops were doing their jobs (as measured by arrests and other actions) and to see at a glance how precincts were doing with respect to each other.  No one's saying on TV nowadays that people who go out for a walk should carry a $20 bill to hand over to someone who (you can foresee) will block your way and demand money.  No one's bashing their way along a block of parked cars, stealing the radios, or just vandalizing them for the heck of it.  This is not to say that Giuliani did it alone, or that he did it perfectly, or that there were no costs.  The police sometimes saw the population as hostiles to be policed.  Nor does it address why and how Giuliani went off the deep end after his time in office.  But the city that this century inherited from him is safe because of the regime he ran.

Bed-Stuy, Fort Greene, Williamsburg, Greenpoint, DUMBO, Downton Brooklyn, Crown Heights, Gowanus, Long Island City, Mott Haven, Times Square, Harlem, Lower East Side . . .  these are neighborhoods that could have described as physically dangerous, desolate ghost towns at night or simply  post-industrial wastelands.  

NYC is as expensive as ever but you might say its a victim of its own success.  There's a tension there of course, as gentrification makes those neighborhoods much less affordable.  But that's a losing battle.  

You can't seriously try to sabotage economic growth for the sake of leveling-down equality.  Because leveling-down equality in our nation's premiere city doesn't make sense.  All those neighborhoods above have been demographically transformed several times over during the past 150 years. The populations migrations in and out have been completely fluid--no one has a permanent claim on them.

comments.name: DC
comments.body:
Some readers wonder why Le Pen is running for the 4th time when she has failed 3 times already. 

French politics work differently than the American version.

In France it is not unheard of to run and fail a couple of times before being elected President. Mitterrand was elected President on the *third* try (1965, 1974, 1981). Chirac as well (1981, 1988, 1995). They both went on to win reelection (Mitterrand in 1988 and Chirac in 2002). 

Legal problems aside, there is nothing strange about Le Pen running again. Especially since her party has gone from a fringe phenomenon to now being the most popular in France. Marine Le Pen herself has seen her score go up with every try: in 2012 she got 18% in the first round and was eliminated; in 2017 she got 21% in the first round and went on to get 34% in the second round; in 2022 she got 23% in the first round and 41.5% in the second round.  

Given this linear progression, her huge popularity, and historical precedent, she has every reason to believe she can clutch victory this time. Which obviously doesn't mean she will, but in her universe it makes sense to try again.

articles.summary: Young people are fleeing. Seniors are stuck. Massachusetts needs more starter homes.

comments.name: AttorneyDC
comments.body: True, but more factors are at play. The housing situation in DC is similar to MA. My parents are Boomers living in a large home in Fairfax County. Their neighborhood is flooded with 20-30-year-old children of residents coming to live in their parents' basements, with the average cost of a home on their street at 1.6 million. It's crazy. The reasons are a mix of high interest rates, soaring cost of land, regulations, stepped-up-basis for inherited assets, and others, but it is destroying the inner suburbs and hitting Gen Z really hard.

comments.name: Peg Healy
comments.body:
Townhouses are not appropriate housing development for elders who need to avoid stairs. Nor do elders who want to simplify their lives need to be responsible for gardening, maintenance and repairs. Apartment or condo living of some kind is a good next step as energy winds down.

Single-level condos or apartment buildings next to commercial districts, and near to public transit, are the most efficient way to increase density, yet apartments are not mentioned in this article. Apartments don't have to "ruin the neighborhood": fourplexes can be built to look like large single family homes. Socially, these work best when there is mixed income and mixed ages.

However, the real deterrent to elders selling family houses they have outgrown is the 20+% capital gains tax and income tax due on sale; but if they hold their home until their death, there is a "step up" in basis at death so no capital gains tax is due if the heirs sell, thus preserving family wealth, even if heirs must wait a long time to inherit. Logically, this means elders should rent their family homes to the younger families.

I wish Michelle has provided this information a months ago; it’s probably too late to hire a CPA or tax attorney to make these claims now. The taxpayer can try to do it himself/herself, but it’s going to take a lot of time. It is nearly impossible to get the transcripts from the IRS and prepare everything in the next 2 days. If I filed a Form 2848 to get authorization to get a taxpayer’s transcripts today, I probably wouldn’t get access for a week, unless I called the Practitioner Priority Line and sat on the phone with the IRS for 3 hours. So if you are taxpayer who wants to get this done by Friday, and do you want to hire someone to help you, expect them to charge extra because they will be really scrambling to accomplish this in time. If you do want help from an attorney in the DMV I’d recommend my friends at Kathryn Meyer Esq., Frost Law, or Oakgrove Legal Strategies.

comments.name: MWAnderson
comments.body:
In West African nations this is known as a Harmattan Wind, and is typically a part of their dry season, which runs from late September/October to February/March [it varies a bit].

And while I doubt such will reach the U.S., in Cameroon, Nigeria and other west African nations the Harmattan Wind typically displaces and causes swarms of 'Poppa Bugs,' to inundate populous areas.  These Poppa Bugs are a small, elongated beetle of the Paederus genus; they look like flying ants, black with a red abdomen, and has a toxic substance in its abdomen that causes burns when the beetle is crushed against the skin [resulting in outbreaks of 'Paederus Dermatitis'].

And they tend to show up at night--because of their attraction to bright lights--which inspires those in the know to check their bedding before laying down to sleep.

Saharan dust primarily fertilizes the Amazon by delivering phosphorus, an essential nutrient for plant growth, and is from the Bodélé Depression in Chad, an ancient, dried lakebed where rock minerals are highly concentrated.  (I've seen a NOVA documentary on this, it was very interesting.)

ANYWAY, the dust is NOT BAD, it's actually beneficial, just will create that haze they are talking about.

But, as all the individuals who are poor money managers and end up broke in retirement, there will be an outcry to set up a government funded program to pick up the tab for them without a corresponding tax plan to pay for it. The issue is the political reluctance to fix the funding side of Social Security while kicking the can down the road to a crisis the politicians hope will happen after they leave office with their own government provided retirement.

comments.name: texasindie

Every structural steel project undergoes changes during the detailing process; erection and shop plans are the final finish product, not the Engineer's design drawings. 

It's a complex process where senior drafts-people submit questions to the Engineer regarding steel design plan discrepancies, and then the Engineer provides the solutions.  Then the shop detail drawings are submitted for approval - every beam, every column and brace detailed out with all the connections, welds and bolts. the Engineer reviews each drawing and stamps their approval or lists the required changes and requests the drawings be resubmitted before fabrication begins. 

Hard to believe, in this age of computer modeling and stress analysis, that they built a structural 3D engineering model from the original steel erection plans and shop details and suffered this kind of structural failure.

comments.name: stephan morrow
comments.body:
I had a background in appreciation of modern art as far back as a naive Stuyvesant H.S. student where MOMA's cafe was our candy store to hang out in after school. Can't explain it & never ran across many fellow Stuyvesantians there. Strictly a solo trip but I didn't mind. I even, dare I say, became a self-appointed docent when a group of people ended up in front of a painting: I was off to the races. (the level of ignorance of so many attendees was impressive - even younger ones who just wanted to be photographed in front of a canvas. ) Anyway, in my year at The Freshman Grad Division: an experimental program where the most naive students were given graduate faculty to see what the combination would produce - I ran across Marcia Tucker - as an art history lecturer and she ushered myself and other lucky acolytes into a deeper appreciation of classical art: all the greats - Botticelli,Titian,   Rembrandt (striking anecdote was how @ 62 he had married his 14 yr old maid - after he had lost his fame & fortune.). But we stayed in touch & became good friends. Really. So one day we were crossing Forty Deuce & the pavement was wet & reflecting the red & green traffic lights: Me: "So is that art?". She "Yes. Why not? What defines art or beauty for that matter?". And on and on. So it's interesting how that question (brought up here) lingers still. 
My question now is "But 'is it great?' e.g. banana peels. (Skeptical. Will it be worshipped 20 yrs from now?) 
Art Dir
Grt Am Play Series

Lastly is the issue of what constitutes exploitation - if the workers are exploitable because they are here illegally, it is not clear if that is exploitation or just the economics of the shadow market of illegal workers. Do the workers themselves think they are being cheated? Perhaps they understand that working illegally means lower wages but they are nevertheless grateful for a job.

There is a lot going on here and I would not do anything unless you witness abuse or unsafe working conditions.

How can anyone determine whether news is true or false before all the facts are known? The government should not unnecessarily restrict or suppress the public's right to know or the fundamental right to freedom of speech. Instead, it should communicate clearly, transparently, and accurately about important issues rather than silence differing voices or limit people's rights.

Otherwise, what distinguishes a free society from countries where the government tightly controls information, e.g., N. Korea, Venezuela?

If a law is enacted to penalize the publication of information later determined to be true, then the government should bear full responsibility for the consequences. If a news report is ultimately proven accurate, those who were penalized should be fully compensated for all financial losses and other damages they suffered during the entire period before the truth was established.

What we are seeing in the Pacific is the ripple effect of a retreating U.S. hegemony and increasingly ambiguous commitments to allies that once placed complete trust in the alliance. Middle powers like Australia and Japan, which traditionally relied on U.S. security guarantees, are now losing their strategic orientation in a multipolar world. Fear and uncertainty naturally come first.

Australia, in particular, feels increasingly alone as the only major Anglo-Saxon nation in the region besides NZ. China is stepping into Australia's comfort zone simply because it now can. That doesn't mean China views Australia as a primary threat—far from it. Japan is a bit more concerning for Beijing, although the balance of power still heavily favors China.

China's growing presence in the Pacific is all about military expansion. I think the Chinese leadership has also learned from Japan's failure in World War II. Much of what we see today is deterrence-building aimed primarily at the US in prep for any move against TW. I don't think sending a few Australian or Japanese warships would fundamentally change China's calculations.

Australia needs to learn from its Asian neighbors and decide whether it sees itself primarily as an Asia-Pacific nation or an Anglo-Saxon nation. The same question applies to Japan. Pragmatism has long been the key to how Asian civilization states have coexisted for millennia, and that lesson may become increasingly relevant in the years ahead.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
Thanks for reporting on this subject. It's sad to see the terrible effect on sea life from these ocean heat waves. And this ocean heat has other grave implications.

There are parts of the system that are already out of our hands. And those parts are related to the ocean. Because we know that we’ve already put a lot of heat content into the ocean. 

And in the case of the Antarctic Ice Sheet, regarding the marine based ice which is very sensitive to ocean temperatures—West Antarctica 3.3 meters of sea level rise equivalent of ice, East Antarctica 19 meters—we are committed to some response of the ice sheet to the heat that has already gone into the ocean. And Greenland has around 3 meters worth of marine based ice as well.

How much response? According to the paleoclimate record at 1.5-2°C above preindustrial temperature around 6-9 meters of sea level rise (we’re likely already committed to at least 2°C)
At 3°C, tens of meters eventually.

Times scales are the big question and the community in general has been conservative with time scales.

It was about 2008 that I learned the the AMNH had a collection of toi moko, Maori preserved heads. I sent a pitch to a few publications in New York to write an article about it, and nobody was interested. I was told it wasn't topical. My reply was that a museum having human remains that were stolen was topical at any time, especially considering those remains were the great-grandparents of people living today.

The AMNH eventually repatriated the toi moko. I'm glad it's giving back the hair samples now. But there's still a lot out there. I visited the Mutter Museum in Philadelphia a few years ago and was shocked how many of the anatomical exhibits there were clearly obtained without consent, often the consequence of grave robbing.
